newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh dealers see slip in long T-bill yields.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh dealers see slip in long T-bill yields.

text.p: Yields on Kazakh three-month Treasury bills are likely to be roughly unchanged later this week, while 12-month T-bills could fall by up to two percentage points, dealers said on Sunday.
Sunday is a normal working day in the former Soviet republic after a long May Day holiday.
Kazakhstan's finance ministry is offering 400 million tenge of 12-month MKM discount T-bills on Monday and 600 million tenge of three-month paper on Tuesday.
The yield on three-month T-bills fell to 20.04 percent annual at their last auction on April 29 from 21.72 percent on April 22. Demand was 1.26 billion tenge against 600 million on offer.
The yield on 12-month paper fell to 26.17 percent at the last auction on April 7 from 27.49 percent on March 10. Demand was 1.4 billion tenge against 350 million tenge on offer.
"I do not see lower yields on three-month paper. Today's 20 percent is already the minimal level," said Lyudmila Pogulyayeva, dealer at ABN AMRO Bank Kazakhstan.
She said the foreign interest in Kazakh T-bills remains steady. "But foreign investors also seem uninterested in lower yields," she added.
Baizhan Gabdullin of Alfabank Kazakhstan said he also expected the yield on three-month paper to be steady at around 20 percent.
But yields on 12-month paper could fall to 24-25 percent annual, Pogulyayeva said.

She said last week the National Bank did not hold auctions of its short-term notes issued regularly to sterilise the money supply and support the rate of the national currency, and no note auctions are being held later this week.

"At the same time, the finance ministry has recently made big repayments on several note and T-bill auctions worth around 2.5 billion tenge...Many local banks might prefer to invest in longer-term T-bills with higher yields," she said.
Gabdullin said the yield on 12-month T-bills could fall even to 22.5-23.0 percent.
"The tendency towards lower yields continues due to big demand (for longer-term paper) -- there is a lot of money in the market," he said, also noting recent large repayments of notes and T-bills.
